mcqs.question: What's the main cost of single-leader replication compared to multi-leader or leaderless?
options: Write throughput and write availability are both capped by the single leader, and its failure blocks writes until failover completes
It cannot serve reads from more than one node
It requires every follower to also accept writes
It's impossible to use with relational databases
mcqs.explanation: Single-leader replication funnels every write through one node, capping throughput and creating a temporary write outage on leader failure. It scales reads fine across followers, followers don't accept writes by definition, and it's the default for Postgres/MySQL.

mcqs.question: Why does multi-leader replication introduce conflicts that single-leader replication never has to deal with?
options: Multi-leader systems use slower disks than single-leader systems
More than one node can accept a write to the same record independently, so two writes can race with no single point that ordered them
Multi-leader systems don't support read replicas
Conflicts only happen due to network latency, not the number of leaders
mcqs.explanation: With multiple independent write-acceptors, two writes to the same record can happen concurrently with nothing enforcing an order between them — that's the structural source of conflicts. It isn't about disk speed or read replicas, and the root cause is the multiple write points, not latency alone.

mcqs.question: A system needs low-latency local writes in three separate regions and can tolerate resolving occasional write conflicts. Which replication strategy fits best?
options: Single-leader, with all three regions writing to one central leader
Multi-leader, with one leader per region
No replication at all, to avoid conflicts entirely
Single-leader, but with the leader migrated to a new region every hour
mcqs.explanation: Multi-leader is designed exactly for this case: each region gets a local leader for fast writes, at the cost of needing conflict resolution. A single central leader reintroduces cross-region write latency, no replication risks data loss, and migrating the leader hourly doesn't solve the latency problem for two of the three regions.

mcqs.question: A team adds a second leader in another region for lower write latency, with no conflict resolution strategy decided. What's the likely outcome?
options: Nothing changes, since replication automatically prevents conflicting writes
Writes will fail loudly whenever a conflict occurs, alerting the team immediately
The system will likely fall back to something crude like last-write-wins, silently discarding one of two conflicting updates
The second leader will simply refuse to accept any writes until a policy is set
mcqs.explanation: Without an explicit strategy, most systems default to a crude resolution like last-write-wins, which silently drops one update rather than failing loudly or refusing writes. Replication doesn't prevent concurrent writes on its own — that's exactly what multi-leader allows.

mcqs.question: Why can a G-counter CRDT merge concurrent increments from two replicas without any conflict resolution step?
options: Because each replica tracks its own increment count separately, and the total is just the sum across replicas — merging is taking the max per replica and adding, which never loses an increment
Because CRDTs block concurrent writes from happening at all
Because G-counters only allow one replica to write at any given time
Because the counter periodically resets to zero to avoid drift
mcqs.explanation: A G-counter's structure (per-replica counts summed for the total) makes concurrent increments commutative and mergeable by construction — there's no conflict to resolve because no increment is ever overwritten. It doesn't block concurrency, restrict writes to one replica, or reset periodically.
